# Diagnosing Persistent High Engine Temperature on a Nissan Micra K12

A Nissan Micra K12 with the CR10DE engine running hot regardless of driving conditions presents a classic thermal management failure. The fact that the vehicle is overheating whether idling or under load narrows the differential significantly, pointing toward a loss of heat exchange capacity or a blockage in the cooling circuit rather than an intermittent sensor glitch. Your initial diagnostic scan indicated hard starting and high fuel consumption, leading to the replacement of the crankshaft position sensor. While that component is critical for ignition timing and idle control, its failure does not typically manifest as sustained thermal runaway. The lack of positive effect after replacing the sensor confirms that the root cause lies elsewhere in the cooling system or engine management logic.

The most glaring piece of evidence you discovered is that the thermostat has been removed. This is a critical architectural error in the cooling loop. Most Nissan engines, including the 1.0L CR10DE, utilize an electric water pump coupled with a thermostatic valve to regulate coolant flow. When the thermostat is absent, the system loses its ability to maintain a specific operating temperature threshold. Instead of circulating coolant through the engine block only when it reaches approximately 86Â°C (187Â°F), the pump continuously circulates coolant through the radiator whenever the electric pump engages.

This creates two distinct problems depending on the ambient conditions. In cold weather, the engine will struggle to reach its optimal operating temperature because the thermostat's "closed" position is missing. However, in hot weather or during high-load driving, this setup becomes dangerous. Without the restriction provided by the closed thermostat, the entire volume of coolant flows through the radiator even when the engine is cold, but more critically, it prevents the system from building the necessary thermal mass to protect the cylinder head gasket during peak heat loads.

The removal of the thermostat also disrupts the pressure dynamics within the cooling system. Modern cooling systems rely on a pressurized environment, maintained by the radiator cap, to raise the boiling point of the coolant (often to roughly 120Â°C). If the thermostat is gone and the system relies solely on the electric pump's flow rate against the open radiator neck, you risk cavitation or localized hot spots if the flow velocity isn't perfectly balanced. Furthermore, many K12 engines have a specific design where the thermostat housing acts as a reservoir for the coolant level sensor. Without this component in its designated slot, air pockets can form more easily, leading to false high-temperature readings from the ECT (Engine Coolant Temperature) sensor.

To resolve this, you must reinstall a functional thermostat rated for the 1.0L engine. Do not substitute it with a generic part; ensure the temperature rating matches the factory specification, typically around 86Â°C. Additionally, inspect the upper and lower radiator hoses for softness or collapse, as high flow rates without thermal regulation can exacerbate hose fatigue. If the coolant has been running without the thermostat for an extended period, perform a thorough flush to remove any sludge that may have settled when the system was constantly in "open" circulation mode.

Finally, verify the operation of the electric water pump. Since the cooling loop is now unregulated by the thermostat, the pump must work harder to maintain flow, potentially shortening its lifespan. If the pump is failing, you are facing a cascading failure where the overheating damages the head gasket, leading to coolant loss and white smoke from the exhaust. Addressing the missing thermostat is the immediate fix, but monitoring the cooling fan control logic is also advisable, as the ECU may not engage the fans correctly if it never sees the engine enter its normal thermal range due to the missing valve.
